newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Violent end to S. Korean strikes appears inevitable.
newsitem.headline: Violent end to S. Korean strikes appears inevitable.

text.p: A violent end to South Korean strikes appears inevitable as militant union leaders seek to turn stoppages into a political fight against President Kim Young-sam in an election year, analysts say on Wednesday.

After unions rejected dialogue, Kim has no alternative other than to crack down on leaders spearheading wildcat srikes disrupting key export industries before campaigns begin for December's presidential elections, they said.
"If strike leaders are arrested, then unions will select new leaders to continue protests," said Kim Young-jin, fellow at Korea University's institute for labour affairs.
"But the government seems to believe it could isolate strike leaders from other workers who are not politically oriented."
Striking unionists demanding the repeal of a controversial labour law have vowed to prolong their protests until December and defeat the candidate of the ruling New Korea Party.
"The government will have to give up power if it met union demands," an Asian diplomat said. "But the elated unions leaders are not in a mood to accept an easy compromise."
Despite failure to deliver their threats to organise nationwide strikes, union leaders have claimed a victory in a race to win public opionion against the government.
Surveys showed most South Koreans opposed the railroading of the labour bill allowing companies to lay off workers, replace striking unionists and introduce flexible working hours.
The government could no longer tolerate the opposition trying to capitalise on the crisis by slamming the labour law, the Asian diplomat said.
About 2,000 professors, lawyers, priests and human rights campaigners have joined the opposition in a call for a revision of the law, branding the president as an authoritarian.
Some analysts warned of possible mayhem and protracted strikes if workers are seriously injured during police arrests.
"South Korean workers are very emotional and nobody can predict the outcome if there are serious injuries," said Lee Hahn-koo, head of the private Daewoo Research Institute.
He urged a compromise between the government and unions.
"It is not the content of the law that people oppose but the secretive, hardline method the ruling party used to pass the bill," Lee said.
The New Korea Party rammed the controversial labour law through parliament on December 26 in a six-minute dawn session when opposition deputies were asleep.
A senior ruling party official said policymakers had expected limited strikes.
"But strikes continue longer than we had earlier expected and we could not let unions stage illegal activities until spring when wage negotiations are due to begin," he said.
State prosecutors on Wednesday issued an ultimatum to seven leaders of the outlawed Korean Confedeation of Trade Unions to drop industrial action immediately or face arrest.
The prosecution has arrest warrants on the seven sheltering in a Seoul cathedral to organise nationwide strikes.

Trade Minister Ahn Kwang-koo warned that the labour strife which have crippled key export industries could make it harder for the country to control its trade deficit, which snowballed to $20 billion last year from $10.06 billion in 1995.
Analysts said the government was setting a stage for a crackdown amid signs that strikes are faltering.

Despite the call for all-out strikes by the confederation and the officially-sactioned Federation of Korean Trade Unions, Seoul was largely unaffected by stoppages, with buses, subways and other public services running normally.
Labour expert Kim of Korea University said: "The ruling camp can't afford to let the labour issue damage its election prospects.
"It will probably offer some carrots to workers later in the form of special legislation and may recognise the confederation immediately as a compromise," he added.
